lines.text: Imagine a sound you cannot escape. A low, steady rumble, like a truck idling somewhere down the road. You step outside. Nothing. You drive away. It follows. And the person next to you hears nothing at all.

This is the Taos Hum. Hundreds of people have described it. Scientists spent a week hunting for it with the best instruments in the country. And the answer they found is stranger than any alien story.
Tonight we run it as a listening survey. Five stations. Every claim gets measured, then scored.
Station one, the town. Station two, the instruments. Three, the people who hear it. Four, the suspects. Five, the real explanation.
The question is simple. Is the hum a secret machine, a signal from something else, or something inside us? Let's listen.
Station one. The town. Taos, New Mexico, a high desert town of artists, adobe walls and mountain light. Not a place anyone would call noisy.
In the spring of nineteen ninety-one, residents began to complain of a low droning sound. Not every night. Not every person. But enough to get talked about.
They described it as a diesel engine idling far away. Some felt it in their chest. Some said it made them dizzy, or kept them awake for months.
Local papers picked up the story. Neighbours compared notes. A pattern emerged: the sound was louder indoors, louder at night, and worse in quiet rooms.
Some people had heard hums elsewhere before. Hueytown, Alabama. Kokomo, Indiana. Even England, in the nineteen seventies. But Taos was the first to make national news.
By nineteen ninety-three, the complaints reached Washington. Members of Congress asked for an official investigation into a sound that nobody could record.
The request was granted. A real, funded, scientific hunt for the Taos Hum was about to begin.
Teams from the University of New Mexico, Sandia National Laboratories, Los Alamos and an Air Force research lab arrived in Taos that summer.
Their plan: surround the town with every instrument that could hear, feel or detect a signal. If the hum existed, they would find it.
Station two. The instruments. First, microphones. Sensitive enough to pick up sounds far below the quietest whisper, set up in the homes of people who said they heard it.
The signal they were hunting would sit between thirty and eighty hertz. That is deep bass, the range of a distant engine or a big speaker's lowest note.
Second, geophones, buried in the ground, to catch vibrations travelling through rock. If the hum came from underground machinery, these would feel it.
Third, electromagnetic detectors, in case it was a radio signal, a power line, or something transmitting. They swept every band they could.
A week of nights in the field. Teams working in shifts, in homes, in yards, on hillsides. Hundreds of hours of data.
The results came back. No sound at the frequencies people described. Nothing above the background noise, even with a detector able to see far below normal hearing.
Seismic sensors recorded no unusual vibration. Electromagnetic sweeps found no matching signal. The instruments heard nothing. Not a whisper.
The geophones did catch something once: a gopher, digging nearby. That was the most dramatic discovery of the field study.
The team published their findings in a scientific journal. Their conclusion was careful: no source found, but the people reporting it were sincere.
So if the machines heard nothing, who was hearing something? That is the part of the story that gets interesting.
Station three. The hearers. The researchers mailed out a survey, eight thousand forms, to find out who was hearing the hum, and what they heard.
About fourteen hundred people answered. A hundred and sixty one said they heard the hum. That is about two percent of the respondents.
Most hearers were between thirty and fifty-nine years old. Most said they heard it daily. Nearly three quarters described the same thing: an idling diesel engine.
One surprise. About one in five heard it more than fifty miles from Taos. It was not a place. It followed the person.
Then came a clever test. Hearers listened to a tone generator and tuned it until it matched what they heard. The matches clustered between thirty-two and eighty hertz.
The sound also pulsed, slowly, between half a beat and two beats every second. A slow throb, like breathing, or a heartbeat, or a distant engine.
Some hearers said the hum drove them to despair. Some moved house. A few said it was the worst thing they had ever lived with.
Stories spread that dogs reacted to it too. We could find no solid record of that. It remains an unverified legend, not evidence.
Meanwhile, doctors noticed something else. Many hearers had no hearing loss. Some had trouble sleeping. Some were under heavy stress.
A sound that is real to the person, but invisible to the machines. Hold that thought. Now to the suspects.
Station four. The suspects. Every theory gets a line-up. Evidence in one column, imagination in the other.
Suspect one. The military. The favourite theory said the hum came from very low frequency radio that the navy uses to talk to submarines.
The idea sounds neat. But those signals are radio, not sound. Radio waves cannot be heard by human ears, and the survey found no matching radio signal in Taos.
Suspect two. HAARP, the Alaska research array. People love it as a culprit. But it sits more than three thousand miles away, and its output does not make audible bass.
Suspect three. Industry. Factories, pipelines, pumps and power plants do make low hums. In Kokomo, Indiana, investigators found real machines behind some complaints.
Taos has no big factory. But low frequency sound travels very far, and a distant compressor can sound like nothing at all to a microphone, yet loud in a room.
Suspect four. The one you were waiting for. An alien base, a hidden underground facility, a craft humming beneath the mountains.
We checked. No record, no photograph, no measurement, no witness. It is a story, told because the hum has no known source. Nothing more.
And think about the logic. A secret alien base would be heard by everyone nearby. Not two percent. Not a few dozen. Everyone.
Suspect five. The human ear itself. And this one is not a theory. It is a medical fact that the ear can make its own sounds.
Tinnitus is the best known. A ringing, or a hum, or a buzz, with no outside source. Millions of people live with it, and it can sound like anything.
There are also spontaneous otoacoustic emissions: tiny sounds the inner ear itself produces. In a quiet room at night, some people can sense them.
But the ear cannot explain everything. Others heard it far from home, and some had perfect hearing. So what else is there?
Station five. The real explanation. And it is not one answer. It is a stack of small ones, each with evidence.
One. Real low frequency noise exists in the world, and some people are simply more sensitive to it. Traffic, pumps, wind turbines, even electrical gear.
Low bass travels through walls and ground, and hardly fades with distance. A noise made miles away can appear in your bedroom and nowhere else.
Two. In silence, the brain turns up its gain. A hum you could not hear at noon becomes loud at three in the morning.
Three. Attention and worry. Once you notice a sound, you cannot unnotice it. The more you listen, the louder it seems. Researchers see this loop in many chronic sounds.
Four. Stress and poor sleep. Many hearers were under pressure, and many slept badly. That does not make the sound imaginary. It makes it a real experience with a real cause.
And five. Taos itself. A quiet town in a deep valley, where distant sounds carry and nights are very still. A perfect place to notice a hum.
None of this proves the answer for every case. A few hearers may be picking up a real industrial source somewhere. The honest word is, mostly solved, partly open.
Later studies elsewhere found the same pattern: hearers, no source, nothing on the instruments. The Taos hum became a model case in acoustic research.
It also taught a hard lesson. When science finds nothing, that does not mean the person is lying. It can mean we are measuring the wrong thing.
If you hear a hum yourself, you are not crazy, and you are not alone. A doctor and a quiet, steady sleep routine can help more than any conspiracy.
So now we score every claim. Evidence on one side, theory on the other. The Taos Hum, put on trial.
One last thing before the scorecard. The most chilling part of the hum was never the sound. It was how alone it made people feel.
Debrief. Time to score the Taos Hum.

People report a real hum, hundreds of cases, in many places: evidence. No source found by a week of instruments: evidence. The same pattern in a survey, about two percent hearing it: evidence. Ear and brain explanations: likely.
Navy submarine radio: debunked as sound. HAARP: debunked. A secret alien base: no evidence. Industrial noise in some cases: partly open.
The verdict. Not aliens, not a weapon. A real experience, from real ears and minds, probably helped along by distant low noise and a very quiet night. Mostly explained, never fully closed.
And that may be the most human mystery of all. A sound that only some of us can hear, and that no machine can prove.
Next case: an ancient stone circle, a vanished builders' secret, and the strange sounds people say echo through it. What were they listening for?
Do you hear a hum? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
